item.title: 3D Structure Analysis from XAS using Diffusion Models
item.description: The local three-dimensional (3D) atomic structure of materials and molecules can be interrogated by X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), a powerful analytical technique. Here, we introduce a diffusionmodel-based approach that rapidly infers candidate 3D structures from X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) data. The method is validated on multi-element hard X-ray XAS datasets and generalizes across a broad range of molecular and material systems without imposing restrictions on the number of constituent element types. Compared with multi-round iterative optimization methods for 3D structure determination that use a structure-to-spectrum model as the core spectral calculation engine, our approach substantially improves data analysis efficiency, enabling 3D structure determination within a few reverse diffusion steps. On low-end consumer GPUs, 3D structure analysis takes 0.5–5s. We anticipate that this method will significantly facilitate online data analysis at beamlines and associated real-time experimental planning and optimization, enable batch screening of atomic-level 3D structures, and improve the efficiency of conventional 3D structure fitting.

item.title: AI Agents as supporting infrastructure for all-solid-state battery development
item.description: Materials discovery increasingly depends on a multiscale ecosystem of simulations, experiments, and shared facilities, yet advances in individual AI tools do not by themselves connect the decisions that link these components. This gap is especially severe in all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), whose development couples electrochemical performance to interfacial stability, mechanics, processing, manufacturability, reliability, safety, and cost. Here we argue that AI agents could support ASSB development toward commercial viability by maintaining a shared decision–evidence state that links materials discovery and optimization to cell-level validation and manufacturing constraints. We develop this argument through three complementary dimensions of scientific agency: coordination across heterogeneous resources, method augmentation across models and scales, and project-level adaptation over time. Cross-domain demonstrations establish several relevant capability primitives, including stateful tool planning, task execution, and delegated analysis. Agents should therefore be evaluated as supporting infrastructure for concurrent ASSB engineering rather than as autonomous replacements for scientific expertise. Their value ultimately lies in driving materials development in the context of interfaces, cell architectures, and manufacturing processes toward the performance, reliability, safety, and cost requirements of ASSB commercialization. context & scale Commercializing all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) requires more than identifying high-performing materials: ion transport, interphase chemistry, mechanics, processing, cell architecture, reliability, safety, and cost impose coupled constraints that can invalidate otherwise promising candidates. This Perspective argues that AI agents could serve as auditable infrastructure, maintaining a decision-evidence state that connects objectives, specimen histories, models, uncertainties, actions, and validation to support ASSB development. Such infrastructure could broaden research across instruments and engineering stages, strengthen validation by linking atomistic, mesoscale, continuum, and experimental descriptions, and preserve evidence and revisions throughout development cycles. Future efforts should move beyond task-level demonstrations toward systematic ASSB development, establishing whether agents can contribute to the development of reliable and economically viable ASSB systems.

item.title: Order-Disorder Phase Transitions and Site Occupancy Pattern in Fe1.5Ni1.5Ga4 Unravelled by Resonant Scattering
item.description: The insufficient X-ray scattering contrast and similar neutron scattering cross-sections of Fe and Ni render the accurate determination of ‘coloring scheme’ ambiguous in the vacancy ordered 43 −superstructure of CsCl-related phase Fe1.5Ni1.5Ga4. Therefore, to overcome this limitation, X-ray resonance diffraction near the K-absorption edge of Fe has been utilized for the accurate site occupancy pattern of Fe and Ni in the structure of Fe1.5Ni1.5Ga4. Measurements on three independently annealed samples with progressively longer annealing times revealed no evidence of atomic ordering, instead, Fe prefers to partially occupy the Ni site (48𝑔 Wyckoff site) in the structure of binary Ni3Ga4 (𝐼𝑎3̅𝑑 space group, 𝑎 =11.52 Å). The vacancy ordering present at the 16𝑏 site drives the lattice distortion in the structure. Upon heating to ~955 K, the room-temperature (RT) structure transforms to the 2.9 Å CsCl-type structure (𝑃𝑚3̅𝑚 space group), where Fe, Ni and vacancy are randomly distributed suppressing the lattice distortions. DFT based calculations on the hypothetical ordered model predict a ferromagnetic ground state with non-magnetic and antiferromagnetic states lying very close to it in energy. This near-degeneracy points to a highly complex magnetic energy landscape with competing ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, which explains the experimentally observed spin-glass behavior.

item.title: A Scoping Review of Diffusion-Based De Novo Molecular Generation: Architectures, Evaluation, and Open Challenges for Computational Drug Discovery
item.description: Diffusion models form the bulk of generative frameworks used in de novo molecular design, yet the literature remains fragmented across model formulations, molecular representations, and generative tasks, and inadequate systematic accounts exist of how these models are steered towards molecules with desired properties, an aspect of drug discovery that is paramount to acceptance. We present a scoping review of diffusion-based neural networks applied in de novo drug discovery between 2020 and 2026. Following the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) protocol, we categorise the literature into non-mutually exclusive themes covering methodological contributions, conditioning mechanisms, molecular representations, symmetries, and multi-modal integrations, and outline the datasets and evaluation metrics used throughout. Three findings emerge. First, diffusion did not displace earlier architectures so much as absorb them: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Autoencoders, and Transformers persist as backbones, and what changed was the training objective. Second, conditioning strategies reduce to structural anchoring, target-aware biochemical conditioning, property-driven steering, and multimodal latent conditioning; within these, the point in the reverse trajectory at which a conditioning signal is applied is a design variable distinct from the signal itself. Third, evaluation remains unstandardised across frameworks, datasets, and definitions. We identify the resulting gaps in controllability and interpretability as the central open challenge for conditioned molecular generation and outline the direction to ease them as this would enable generation of molecules that match the preferred property profiles.

item.title: Facile Nitrogen Doping of Electrospun Mesoporous Carbon Nanofibers via Urea Addition for Polysulfide-Confining Li-S Cathodes and Interlayers
item.description: Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries offer high theoretical capacity, but polysulfide dissolution and shuttling cause rapid capacity fade. Nitrogen functional groups can anchor polysulfides, yet in our previous work, introducing them through a post-carbonization cyclized-PAN treatment sacrificed much of the carbon nanofiber (CNF) mesoporosity, and Nfunctionalizing both cathode and interlayer performed worst. Here, nitrogen is introduced during fiber formation by adding urea to a PAN/PMMA precursor before gas-assisted electrospinning, followed by stabilization, carbonization, and CO2 activation. This gives N-doped mesoporous CNFs with better control over the balance between nitrogen content and pore structure. Across four cathode/interlayer combinations ,every cell with at least one N-doped component outperformed the undoped cell. The N-doped cathode with N-doped interlayer performed best, delivering 1271 mAh g-1 at 2C with the lowest charge-transfer resistance (8 Ω vs. 11 Ω undoped). Post-mortem XPS revealed Li-N interactions and polysulfide retention, strongest in the interlayers. Precursor-level nitrogen doping is therefore an effective route to Li-S cathodes and interlayers that balance nitrogen and mesoporosity.

item.title: C2 Homologation of Alkenes with Programmable Substitution
item.description: Alkene homologation represents an efficient strategy for upgrading commodity olefins and expediting the synthesis of their longer homologues. However, current alkene homologation methodologies are limited to the access to terminal alkenes. Herein, we report a radical‑based approach that enables C2 homologation of alkenes with programmable substitution patterns. This transformation features a radical hydro-alkylation of alkenes using bromomethylphosphonium hexafluorophosphate as an electrophilic carbon radical precursor. The resulting phosphonium salt, bearing a C1-extended chain, undergoes Wittig olefination with inexpensive aldehyde/ketone to deliver C2-elongated terminal/1,2-/1,1,2-substituted alkenes (>40 examples, up to 99% yield; Z/E up to >20:1, with photocatalytic access to the E-isomers). This protocol exhibits broad functional group tolerance and is applicable to the late-stage modification of bioactive compounds, pharmaceuticals, and liquid crystals. Furthermore, by iteratively combining this C2 method with our previously established C1 homologation, the olefinic chains of complex molecules can be precisely elongated by three, four, or more carbon atoms. Comprehensive mechanistic studies, including DFT calculations and experimental probes, support a radical pathway and identify hydrogen bonding between HFIP and triethylamine, which raises the competing HAT barrier from 8.5 to 13.1 kcal/mol, as the key element that suppresses reductive debromination and channels the radical toward C–C bond formation.

item.title: Techno-Economic and Geospatial Assessment of Distributed Fertilizer Production via Wastewater Ammonia Solar Electrochemical Stripping
item.description: Decentralized alternatives to centralized fertilizer production are needed to reduce supply chain risks, minimize transportation costs, and lower environmental impacts. Solar-powered Electrochemical Stripping (ECS) is an emerging technology that can produce ammonium fertilizer in a distributed manner through wastewater nitrogen recovery. We quantify the fraction of fertilizer demand in the United States that can be met by a wastewater feedstock while minimizing transportation distances, finding that 55% (5.54 Mt N per year) of demand is co-located with sufficient supply from domestic, agricultural, or industrial wastewater. A techno-economic assessment of ECS at scales sufficient to meet localized fertilizer demand estimated breakeven prices of US$8.70/kg N for ammonium sulfate, US$9.69/kg N for ammonium nitrate, and US$31.18/kg N for monoammonium phosphate, and US$12.15/kg N for diammonium phosphate. Integration of the techno-economic model with geospatial analysis found ECS-derived fertilizer prices ranged from 2.2x-5.5x local 2016-2026 retail prices, with ECS performing most competitively in the Pacific U.S. region. Sensitivity analysis showed improving current efficiency, increasing current density, lowering capital cost, and increasing equipment lifetime would have the greatest impact on approaching retail cost parity. This work elucidates pathways and barriers to widespread implementation of wastewater-derived fertilizers and advances United Nations Sustainable Development goals for responsible consumption and production, clean water, and zero hunger.

item.title: Dynamical confinement effects on chromophore photoexcitations in a light-harvesting protein
item.description: Naturally evolved light-harvesting complexes are assembled from highly evolutionarily-conserved sequences of amino acids that form functional chemical pockets for chromophores. The protein environment surrounding the chromophore influences its dynamical structure, which can have consequences for light harvesting efficiency. Here, we explore the impact of the C-phycocyanin protein scaffold on the dynamical structure and photoexcited states of the phycocyanobilin (PCB) chromophore using a combination of molecular dynamics and the ab initio Bethe Salpeter equation approach. We compute low-lying excited states of the PCB chromophore for an ensemble of snapshots from molecular dynamics trajectories, and use a normal mode analysis to understand the nature of thermal displacements of PCB in the confined protein environment. We analyze the excited state energies in terms of one electron and electron-hole contributions, identifying displacement patterns with the strongest exciton-vibrational coupling. Our results provide insight into how thermal motion of the chromophore is altered in protein environments and the resulting impact on photo-excited states, with implications for other natural light harvesting materials.

Single-chirality single-walled carbon nanotubes for electrochemical co-detection of serotonin and dopamine
item.description: Dopamine (DA) and serotonin (5-HT) are neurotransmitters whose dysregulation is associated with neurodegenerative diseases. The influence of single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) chirality on sensing remains underexplored. Mixed-chirality SWC- NTs can limit sensor reproducibility and accuracy. Precise control of electrode material structure may promote more specific surface-analyte interactions, enhancing selectivity. Here, screen-printed carbon electrodes (SPCE) were modified with four SWCNT types: mixed-chirality metallic/semiconducting (m/s), metallic (m), or semiconducting (s) SWCNT, and single-chirality semiconducting (6,5)-SWCNT isolated by aqueous two-phase extraction. Vacuum filtration produced surfactant-free SWCNT layers. Codetection of 5-HT and DA was evaluated using differential pulse voltammetry (DPV). The (6,5)-SWCNT/SPCE gave the largest potential difference (∆E = Ep(5-HT)− Ep(DA)) of 151 ± 4 mV and a peak current ratio (Ip(DA)/Ip(5-HT)) of 0.99 ± 0.23. Corresponding values for unmodified SPCE, m/s-SWCNT/SPCE, m-SWCNT/SPCE, and s-SWCNT/SPCE were 139±10, 145±3, 143±6, and 147±3 mV, and 0.60±0.23, 0.63±0.12, 0.63±0.11, and 0.69±0.01, respectively. The (6,5)-SWCNT/SPCE detected both analytes even when one analyte was present in excess. Between 0.04 and 1 µM, linear responses were obtained for 5-HT alone, DA in the presence of 1 µM 5-HT, and 5-HT in the presence of 1 µM DA, with sensitivities of 0.024 ± 0.002, 0.011 ± 0.001, and 0.024± 0.001 nA/nM, respectively. These results show that SWCNT chirality control improves the electrochemical co-detection of 5-HT and DA.

item.title: Integration of Acoustic Ejection Mass Spectrometry Enables Efficient High Throughput Purification Workflow for Peptides in Discovery Space
item.description: 2 ABSTRACT Modern peptide drug discovery combines mRNA display-derived libraries and iterative optimization of hits using solid phase peptide synthesis (SPPS) during hit-to-lead process. Part of this discovery workflow is the need for sufficient amounts of high-quality peptide targets, free from impurities to support the required preclinical assays. In this context, there is a need for streamlined high throughput purification (HTP) workflow coupled with high throughput analytical assays, enabling faster analysis of large volumes of synthetic peptide libraries for purification to accelerate the discovery process. We have developed and validated an ultra-high throughput (uHT) acoustic ejection mass spectrometry (AEMS) based pre-quality control (QC) triage assay for peptide libraries in HTP process, which achieves a sampling rate of ~2 sec/sample with minimal sample requirement (25- 45 µL) and solvent consumption, and fast data analysis, suitable for large sample size in discovery setting. Sample purity profile of the library provided by the newly developed assay is beneficial for HT identification of samples that will or will not advance to purification, enabling a streamlined, faster process, and immediate decisionmaking. Results from the validation and bridging studies are in agreement with the currently employed low-throughput UPLC-UV/MS based HTP pre-QC assay. Integration of the recently developed AEMS-based pre-QC assay in the HTP workflow using a sample purity cut-off of 15% for go/no-go decision renders a minimal false negative, <6% and a false positive results of <12%, making it applicable for the purpose of vetting which samples should be purified to reduce the overall experimental time and cost resource in the HTP process. The recently developed assay demonstrated the first application of AEMS as a pre-QC step in peptide HTP workflow, and its potential application for broad peptide library screening in drug discovery.

item.title: Recombination-zone position, not charge balance, sets the efficiency ceiling of deep-blue TADF host OLEDs
item.description: Low efficiency in organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) is often blamed on charge balance, yet the device models that could test this are rarely converged or constrained by measured inputs. We solve converged drift–diffusion, transfermatrix and dipole models for three deep-blue thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) phosphine-oxide hosts, S1, S3 and S4, with an open solver verified against a converged commercial reference, and we constrain every hostspecific input by measurement: film optical constants from ellipsometry, film photoluminescence, voltammetric host levels and host transport fitted to quality-gated single-carrier current–voltage data. In every converged model OLED with the fitted transport, and also with a shallow-trap transport alternative and with offsets across their identifiable range, charge balance and host confinement are not the limit. What decides the efficiency is where the recombination zone sits: moving it from the electron-transport interface into the host raises the computed air outcoupling about threefold. The model-conditioned efficiency ceiling is therefore set by zone placement and by the photoluminescence quantum yield, which also fixes the host ranking S1>S4≳S3, and transport engineering becomes an outcoupling lever. Two measurements, thickness-dependent current–voltage and angle-resolved photoluminescence, would pin the remaining model ranges (all device quantities are model outputs).

item.title: Self-Derived Metal/Oxide Interface Engineering via Active Nitrogen Mediation
item.description: Self-derived phase engineering of metal oxides offers a powerful route to create interfaces without introducing foreign metallic elements, yet achieving systematic control over phase transition remains challenging. Here, active nitrogen-mediated phase engineering was demonstrated across various metal oxides (SnO2, ZnO, and TiO2). As a model biphasic material, Sn/SnO2 was investigated where urea thermolysis enabled the progressive formation of metallic Sn while largely preserving the host structure, allowing the Sn0 fraction to be systematically controlled. Temperature-programmed experiments using mass spectrometry and FT-IR revealed the involvement of nitrogen-containing intermediates during urea decomposition and supported their central role in driving phase engineering of SnO2. Density functional theory (DFT) based calculations on a Sn/SnO2 model constructed using a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) revealed electron transfer from metallic Sn to SnO2 and the resulting redistribution of surface electron density. The resulting self-derived Sn/SnO2 biphasic material yields favorable surface chemistry by altered surface oxygen behavior and reactivity translating directly into two applications: enhanced chemoresistive formaldehyde gas sensing under humid conditions with ppb-level detection, as well as improved formate production in electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR). Our results identify active nitrogen as a chemical handle for regulating oxide partial reduction and provide a general framework for the systematic engineering of metal/oxide interfaces.

item.title: Measured Host Optical Constants Shift Deep-Blue OLED Outcoupling by up to 14% (Relative) While Leaving the Stack Design Intact
item.description: Outcoupling designs for organic light-emitting diodes rest on the complex refractive index of every layer, yet host films are often given a constant index without absorption. We show what measured constants change, and what they do not. Variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry of three deep-blue phosphine-oxide host films (S1, S3 and S4), refitted from the raw data with several dispersion models, pins the index of the S1 and S4 films to a model-andspot spread of about ±0.002 (about ±0.004 at 95% once substrate-oxide, incidence-angle and roughness systematics are propagated) and reveals a weak absorption tail in S4 that follows its triphenylamine-centered lowest singlet transition; the S3 film is bracketed. Propagated through a dipole model of a deep-blue stack in which the neat host film is the emitter, the measured constants leave the design itself (best emitter position, optimum electron-transport-layer thickness) unchanged within a few nanometers but shift the predicted outcoupling by up to 14% relative (15.1 against 17.2% at the optimum, about 2 percentage points), with the blue dispersion of the index and, for S4, the absorption tail in the emission band contributing comparably (up to about 7% each). Emitter orientation and the emitter–cathode distance act far more strongly, by factors of 2 to 5. Both films are close to isotropic, yet the calculated transition dipoles of S3 and S4 lie in the molecular plane, so growing these hosts with flat-lying molecules is the clearest route to higher outcoupling, worth about a factor of two in the model.

item.title: Weak-Form Regression Recovers the Delayed-Fluorescence Rate Law from Flash-Lamp Decays with Near-Optimal Precision
item.description: Delayed-fluorescence rates and their temperature laws are how thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) materials are ranked, yet the rate law is usually fixed before the analysis, and flash-lamp decays mix the emission with the excitation profile. We show that weak-form regression, with photon-counting statistics and the excitation built into its features, identifies the rate law as a sequence of linear problems with calibrated uncertainties. With a known pulse the whole record, including the excitation window, is used; otherwise the emission after the window is tested against first-order, bimolecular and dispersive terms, and temperature laws are ranked by bootstrap selection frequency. On synthetic decays with lifetimes of 1–1000 µs the method approaches the expected-Fisher precision benchmark and, with the full covariance of its weak residuals, matches fullrecord Poisson maximum likelihood on identical data, whereas ignoring the excitation tail biases rates by more than an order of magnitude and creates spurious activation in more than half of temperature-independent series. Applied to two deep-blue phosphine-oxide hosts, it shows that the later-window delayed emission is not purely first order and that its effective rate has no resolved thermal activation between 200 and 300 K. For this effective rate the tested single-gap Marcus law with the computed gaps is ruled out as rate limiting, which points to a temperature-independent or smallbarrier channel. An identifiability map and open code let any laboratory check, before reporting, which rate law its instrument can resolve.

item.title: Accelerating the Design of Cu(I) Complexes with Near-Infrared Absorption by Interpretable Machine Learning Approaches
item.description: Metal coordination complexes have emerged as promising molecules because of its interesting optical properties and among them the Cu(I) complexes are one of the most fascinating ones, because it’s combination of optical properties and sustainability at the same time. In this work we show for the first time a combination of quantum chemical and cheminformatics approaches to study the wavelength and oscillator strength as photoluminescence properties in a data set of Cu(I) complexes. As a result, machine learning-based Quantitative Structure-Property Relationship (ML/QSPR) model based on machine learning that can reliably predict the absorption wavelength and oscillator strength of Cu(I) complexes was successfully developed, laying the groundwork for high-throughput virtual screening of Cu(I) complexes optical properties. To explain the differences in absorption wavelengths and oscillator strength across structurally diverse individual Cu(I) complexes, the relation between the models and molecular descriptors was analyzed with patterns revealed positive contributing to the properties like polarizability effects, aliphatic chains connected to heteroatoms, and other with negative influence corresponding to symmetry factors, and molecular size and branching. The squared correlation coefficient values for training and validation were 0.82 and 0.85, respectively. In addition, the applicability domain demonstrated the reliability of the prediction of the obtained models. This combined quantum-chemical and cheminformatics strategy has great potential for rational design of novel Cu(I) complexes with desired optical properties. Furthermore, the described procedures might be applied to a wide variety of copper transition-metal complexes.

item.title: Scientific Symbiosis: Bridging Expertise and Fostering Effective Collaborations with Mass Spectrometrists
item.description: Mass spectrometry (MS) is increasingly used to answer biological questions, yet effective collaboration between mass spectrometrists and researchers in other fields can be limited by differences in terminology, expectations, and familiarity with analytical workflows. This review provides a practical and accessible guide to incorporating MS into biological and environmental research with an emphasis on improving communication and collaboration. In the review, we walk through the MS workflow including defining the scientific question, selecting an analytical approach, sample collection and preparation, instrumental analysis, data processing, quality assessment, and interpretation. Particular attention is given to concepts that commonly create confusion across fields, including quantitative strategies, analytical controls, sample handling, instrument monitoring, and data reporting expectations. We also discuss the respective roles of both experimentalists and mass spectrometrists throughout the research process and highlight areas where early communication can prevent downstream problems. To support real-world application, the review includes a glossary of commonly used MS terminology and a checklist of key considerations for collaborative studies. Together, these resources are intended to make MS workflows more approachable and to foster the kind of scientific symbiosis between researchers and mass spectrometrists that is needed to generate high-quality, interpretable, and meaningful data.

item.title: Ultrafast Charge Separation Controlled by Aromatic Guests in a Perylene Dimer
item.description: Engineering charge separation and recombination through non-covalent interactions offers a powerful route to functional photoactive materials without the need for covalent re-engineering. Here, we investigate the ultrafast excited-state dynamics of host-guest complexes formed between a valinol-bridged perylene diimide (PDI) dimer macrocycle and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) guests using sub-50 femtosecond time resolution transient absorption spectroscopy. Macrocycle complexation with pyrene, perylene, and coronene introduces efficient charge-transfer pathways absent in the free host. Photoexcitation of the PDI dimer host leads to rapid quenching of stimulated emission and sub-picosecond formation of PDI radical anions, providing direct evidence for ultrafast hole transfer from the excited host to the PAH guest. The resulting charge-separated states persist for hundreds of picoseconds to nanoseconds before recombination. Analysis within the Marcus framework reveals that charge separation proceeds in a near-barrierless regime, whereas charge recombination lies deep in the Marcus inverted region, accounting for long-lived radical pair states. These results establish aromatic guest binding as a non-covalent handle for accessing fast hole transfer enabling long-lived charge-separated states in supramolecular donor-acceptor assemblies, relevant to light harvesting, photoredox catalysis and organic electronics.

item.title: Thermal Formation of a Magenta Merocyanine in Ethanol: A Microsolvated SP→TCC→TTC Pathway in a Nitrospiropyran
item.description: Solutions of 5’-methoxy-1’,3’,3’-trimethyl-6-nitrospiro[chromene-2,2’-indoline] in alcohols are intensely pink in the dark, become colorless under white light and recover their color thermally, with Arrhenius activation energies of 101.1± 0.5, 104.9± 1.6 and 105.3± 1.4 kJ mol−1 in ethanol, methanol and acidified ethanol, respectively. The measured process is therefore the thermal formation of the merocyanine (MC) from the photogenerated spiropyran (SP). The absorbance of the equilibrated ethanol solution, combined with the calculated oscillator strength, indicates that MC constitutes only a small fraction of the compound, of the order of a few per cent. item.title: Integrating classical similarity and multitask neural representations
item.description: Background. Computational prediction of compound–target associations can help prioritize hypotheses for experimental investigation. While deep learning architectures are increasingly proposed, their apparent superiority often relies on comparisons against untuned classical baselines or evaluation protocols prone to data leakage. Objective. We present a scaffold-disjoint evaluation benchmark derived from ChEMBL 37 to evaluate multitask neural representations against tuned classical similarity search, and we investigate whether combining both paradigms yields improved ranking performance. Methods. The benchmark comprised 100,000 compounds, 1,979 human single-protein targets, and 139,789 positive associations, partitioned by Bemis–Murcko scaffold into train (70%), validation (10%), and test (20%) sets. All hyperparameters were selected on the validation set. We compared a multitask MLP with a tuned K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN-20) baseline, as well as a hybrid model integrating both representations. Results. On the held-out test set, the tuned KNN-20 achieved a Hits@10 of 0.9335, statistically indistinguishable from the 10-seed multitask MLP ensemble (0.9355; Δ = +0.0021, 95% CI [−0.0012,+0.0052]). However, a hybrid model integrating both representations (40% KNN, 60% MLP) achieved a significantly higher Hits@10 of 0.9426, outperforming both KNN-20 (Δ = +0.0091, 95% CI [+0.0066,+0.0116]) and the MLP alone (Δ = +0.0070, 95% CI [+0.0052,+0.0089]). Conclusions. Our results demonstrate that while complex neural models do not inherently outperform well-tuned classical baselines, they capture complementary information. A hybrid approach combining classical chemical similarity and multitask neural representations yields a modest but statistically significant improvement in ranking performance within this benchmark. This study emphasizes the necessity of rigorous baseline tuning and suggests hybrid architectures as a promising direction for compound–target prediction.

item.title: The Thiolate Shell as a Dynamic Gold Reservoir: Size-Dependent Thermal Restructuring of Gold Nanoclusters from MACE-Based Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics
item.description: Atomically precise thiolate-protected gold nanoclusters are used in catalysis, sensing and nanomedicine, where thermal activation, reaction conditions or local heating can change their atomic structure. Whether the gold–thiolate shell remains a fixed protective layer at elevated temperature, or takes part in the restructuring of the cluster, is still an open question, because first-principles molecular dynamics is limited to small clusters and short times. Here we train MACE-AuSCH, an equivariant machine-learned interatomic potential, on a published density functional theory dataset and validate it against 16 crystallographically characterised clusters (cohesive-energy RMSE of 2.1 meV/atom). We then follow seven Aun(SCH3)m clusters, from Au25 to Au279 and with icosahedral and FCC-derived cores, between 8 and 800 K. In all clusters, the effective stiffness of the Au–S bonds is 3.3 to 7.5 times that of the Au–Au bonds, and the metallic Au–Au network reorganises first while most of the Au–S connectivity is kept. At 500 K, the largest core displacements occur in the FCC-derived Au52 and Au92. At 800 K, Au atoms move in both directions between the metallic core and the staple shell, and the loss of Au–S connectivity generally grows with cluster size, from 3% for Au25 to about 40% for Au144. These results describe the protecting shell as a dynamic reservoir of Au atoms and point to an intracluster route that may precede ligand and metal exchange, fragmentation and sintering.

item.title: LigandFF: an open-source implementation of rule-based atom typing, charge assignment and parameter assignment by analogy
item.description: The CHARMM General Force Field (CGenFF) covers drug-like molecules through an automated assignment program that types atoms, assigns charges from bond-charge increments, and transfers missing bonded parameters from analogous ones with an associated penalty. The algorithms are published, but the program and its two hand-built rule files are distributed only in binary form. We describe LigandFF, an open-source reimplementation built exclusively from the published algorithms and the public CGenFF 5.0 topology, parameter and charge-increment files. LigandFF implements the published ring, resonance and aromaticity perception, the rule language for atom typing, the bond-charge-increment scheme with peratom charge penalties, the penalty-weighted analogy search, halogen lone pairs, and writes CHARMM stream files, PSF files and OpenMM and GROMACS inputs. Its typing rules were written against the CGenFF training molecules, and its substitution-penalty matrices were fitted to 5,787 analogies that the official program recorded in the parameter file. On held-out test splits, LigandFF types 97.4% and 97.8% of two sets of CGenFF training molecules with every atom correct (99.7% and 99.6% of atoms). Replaying the analogies recorded in the parameter file against the database they were made from, it recovers the official program’s choice of source parameter for 92.1% of 1,447 held-out cases. It reproduces the program-5.0 charges and penalties printed in the CGenFF 5.0 supporting information exactly, and all 2,074 benchmark molecules produce systems that build in OpenMM. All references are CGenFF training molecules or outputs of the official program that are already public; agreement with the official program on new drug-like molecules has not been measured. LigandFF is not the official CGenFF program, and its outputs are labelled accordingly.

item.title: Mechanistic Insights into Ascorbate-Mediated Activation of Pt(IV) Prodrugs: Axial-Ligand Modulation of Dissociative Reduction Pathways and Redox Latency
item.description: Pt(IV) coordination compounds act as anticancer prodrugs that are intracellularly reduced to cytotoxic Pt(II) species, a process whose selectivity and kinetics depend critically on the nature of the axial leaving (LL) and bridging (LB) ligands. Using DFT/IEFPCM calculations in water, we examined the ascorbate-mediated reduction of six [PtIV(NH3)2Cl2(LL)(LB)] complexes bearing different axial-ligand combinations of chloride, bromide, and dichloroacetate (DCA): LL/LB = Br/Cl, Cl/Cl, DCA/Cl, as well as DCA/Br, Cl/Br, and Br/Br. For the full series, the mechanistic analysis was therefore focused on the inner-sphere pathway involving nucleophilic attack of the ascorbate enolate at the Cβ center (M2), characterized as concerted yet highly asynchronous. Both axial ligands modulate the activation barrier, charge-transfer efficiency, and Pt-L bond dissociation, but the bridging ligand exerts the dominant effect: LB = chloride derivatives display the highest free-energy barriers (Δ[Δ‡G298] ≈ 2-4 kcal mol-1), high charge-transfer percentages (49%-50%) and later transition states relative to LB = bromide analogs. Additionally, the activation barrier is most strongly associated with the extent of charge transfer and its coupling to Cβ–LB bond formation, rather than the overall bond-structural event. These results suggest that LB primarily determines the dissociative-reduction behavior, while LL provides secondary control, thereby providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how axial-ligand combinations influence redox latency in Pt(IV) scaffolds.

item.title: Reconfigurable Nanoscale Material Display
item.description: Dynamic material arrays that combine programmable reconfiguration with direct structural readout could enable materials that both adapt their spatial organization and represent molecular information. DNA nanotechnology offers exceptional control over nanoscale organization, yet most DNA-templated material arrays are static, whereas dynamic DNA circuits typically rely on indirect ensemble readouts. Here, we present a Reconfigurable Material Display, implemented as REMBRANDT (REconfigurable Material-Based Representation of Addressable Nanoscale Display sTates), a DNA-origami platform that decouples structural assembly from programmable organization of nanoscale cargo. A 5 × 5 array of independently addressable DNA pixels organizes DNA-functionalized nanocargo, including gold nanoparticles, quantum dots, and ferritin, and programmably relocates them without reconstructing the underlying scaffold. Pixel encodings define programmable single- and multi-material display states, whereas DNA strand-displacement reactions rewrite cargo-pixel associations to produce sequential and reversible display-state transformations. Each display state is directly resolved by atomic force microscopy and electron microscopy at single-particle and single-display resolution. Programmable cargo relocation further visualizes predefined matrix operations as dynamically reconfigurable material patterns. By integrating programmable reconfiguration with direct structural readout, REMBRANDT establishes a material display in which molecular information is represented, updated, and visualized through nanocargo organization.

item.title: Sulfur Oxidation State Controls Radical Smiles–Truce Rearrangements through a Switch in Cyclization Selectivity
item.description: The radical Smiles–Truce rearrangement is a powerful strategy for constructing aryl–carbon bonds, although competing ortho addition often limits the utility of conventional S(VI) sulfonamide precursors. Here, we demonstrate that switching to S(IV) sulfinamides enables selective ipso aryl migration while providing a stereochemical handle for asymmetric induction. We report a visible-light-driven nitrogen-centered radical cascade that converts alkene-tethered N-acyl sulfinamides into densely functionalized lactams, fused bicycles, and spirocycles through a desulfinylative Smiles–Truce rearrangement. The transformation accommodates electronically diverse arenes, heteroarenes, and substituted alkenes, affording products in up to 85% yield. Moreover, enantioenriched sulfinamide precursors enable efficient transfer of stereochemical information to the products, with up to 93% enantiospecificity. In contrast to analogous S(VI) sulfonamide reactions, competing ortho dearomatization is not observed. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the S(IV) system disfavors the competing ortho-addition pathway, providing a mechanistic basis for the observed selectivity reversal and establishing sulfinamides as versatile precursors for stereocontrolled radical annulations.

item.title: DNA Directed Chemistry: Scalable Programmed DNA-Encoded Library Synthesis for More Chemically Diverse and Drug-Like Libraries
item.description: DNA-Encoded Libraries (DELs) are indispensable high-throughput platforms in drug discovery, but the widely adopted split-and-pool synthesis method is fundamentally limited: the DNA merely records, rather than directs, the steps of chemistry. This lack of programmatic control imposes mandatory downstream chemistry congruency, restricts structural diversity, and inevitably generates a combinatorial explosion of un-drug-like molecules, hindering both hit-finding and the acquisition of structurally informative data required for machine learning (ML) models. To resolve these core constraints, we developed Programmed DEL Synthesis (PDS), a robust, industrially applicable platform for non-combinatorial DEL construction in which the DNA actively directs the synthesis. PDS is built upon a sort-and-pool mechanism expanded by three key innovations: sequence-specific installation of first building blocks using charged carrier codons, a multinomial encoding strategy that enables libraries exceeding 20 billion unique encodings in three chemical steps, and non-combinatorial germline assembly that allows for the programmatic omission of undesirable building block combinations. We demonstrate the platform with Library i01, a three-step, threepathway library employing 137 trifunctional scaffolds. The design successfully programmed the systematic merging and un-merging of three mutually incompatible reaction pathways: Acid→Aldehyde→Amine, Amine→Aldehyde→Acid, and Aldehyde→Acid→Amine within a single synthesis. Pilot affinity selections against Carbonic Anhydrase (BCA-II) validated the high fidelity of DNA encoding and efficient building block installation across all steps and pathways, confirming the platform's robust utility for selection. PDS transforms chemical congruency and drug-likeness into programmable properties, offering a precise, efficient solution that improves library quality without sacrificing chemical space. Crucially, PDS enables the construction of structurally tailored 2nd Generation DELs needed to provide the high-resolution data required for productive ML-driven active learning cycles, establishing a critical operational link for modern drug development.

item.title: Physicochemical Prioritization of Hypothetical Metal–Organic Frameworks for Experimental Synthesis
item.description: The rapid expansion of AI-driven and computationally designed metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) raises a fundamental question: which hypothetical structures are most likely to be experimentally realized? Here, we develop a physicochemically informed strategy to prioritize MOFs for synthesis by integrating molecular synthetic accessibility, framework geometry, electronic structure, solvent removal stability, and thermodynamic stability through positive–unlabeled learning. Using 9,033 experimentally reported MOFs as examples of realized structures and hypothetical MOFs as candidates with unknown synthesizability, we identify 5 complementary physicochemical descriptors that enable effective prioritization, achieving a source-averaged normalized positive rank of 0.93 by placing experimentally realized MOFs near the top of candidate rankings across held-out database sources. Further analysis reveals that experimentally realized MOFs are enriched at low linker geometric distortion and low energy above the convex hull of competing phases, highlighting complementary geometric and thermodynamic considerations. Moreover, secondary building unit–linker analyses identify specific chemical combinations enriched among highly ranked hypothetical structures. Together, these findings establish a chemically interpretable approach to prioritizing hypothetical MOFs and help bridge the gap between computational materials design and experimental synthesis.

item.title: Accept or abstain? A pre-specified test of reliability gates calibrated on held-out chemistry for molecular property and reaction-yield models
item.description: A molecular property or reaction-yield model is useful to a chemist only when it is right on the query in front of them, yet a model’s uncertainty is rarely checked on chemistry it has not seen. We tested an accept-or-abstain protocol in which a gate, scoring each query by its similarity to the training set and by ensemble spread, returns a prediction only when it accepts the query. The gate’s threshold is set by Learn-then-Test to a target precision on a calibration fold held out by chemistry rather than at random. On public data (23,401 logP values from SangsterLogP with two overlapping external sets, and the Buchwald–Hartwig and Suzuki–Miyaura high-throughput yield datasets), we evaluated eight held-out tests against four hypotheses defined in advance. Ranking queries by the gate’s score lowered the error rate at 30% coverage by 0.16 to 0.35 on seven of the eight tests. At a target precision of 0.8, the calibration fold mattered most for yields: gates calibrated on a random fold accepted almost every reaction with an unseen additive at a precision of 0.59 to 0.75, whereas gates calibrated on held-out additives reached a pooled precision of 0.85 to 0.87 on three of the four tests, at lower coverage. At a target of 0.9, random-fold gates came within 0.05 of the target on three of the four tests. For the random forest, fusing similarity with spread did no better than spread alone, and conformal intervals calibrated on a random fold lost coverage under shift (down to 0.64). On a fluorinated-compound hold-out, the fused score ranked errors no better than chance at 30% coverage, and the held-out-calibrated gate missed its target. All four hypotheses therefore failed their success criteria. In an exploratory analysis, conformal intervals calibrated on the held-out fold recovered coverage on seven of the eight tests, at the cost of wider intervals.
