CI-NEB calculations identify complementary transport anisotropies, with Pd adatom diffusion favored along [11̅0] and oxygen-vacancy migration favored along [001], enabling dynamic defect redistribution within the interparticle region. Statistical trajectory analysis shows that increasing the interparticle oxygen-vacancy fraction from 10% to 30% raises coalescence probability and accelerates bridge and neck nucleation, including along the kinetically less favorable [001] alignment. Time-resolved metrics further show that transient low-coordinated bridge-Pd intermediates precede complete particle merging. Together, these results establish defect–transport coupling as a microscopic mechanism for direction-selective sintering on reduced ceria and suggest that suppressing vacancy enrichment and connectivity in interparticle gaps can improve the stability of oxide-supported metal nanoparticles.

item.title: Guest-guest interactions and their impact on molecular mobility: a simulation study of 5-fluorouracil adsorption and diffusion in hydrophobic zeolites
item.description: Zeolites have been proposed as carrier materials for the storage and controlled release of the anticancer drug 5-fluorouracil (5-FU). Containing both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor groups, 5-FU molecules can form relatively strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Prior work on zeolite beta has shown that guest-guest interaction between co-adsorbed 5-FU molecules reduce their diffusivity at high loadings. However, a systematic assessment of the influence of 5-FU oligomer size and zeolite pore topology is so far lacking. Aiming to fill this gap, the present study employs atomistic simulations at different levels of theory to elucidate the strength of 5-FU−5-FU interactions as well as their impact on diffusion in all-silica zeolites. In the first part, adsorption energies of 5-FU oligomers in four zeolites (FAU, BEA, MOR, MFI frameworks) are computed with dispersion-corrected density functional theory (DFT) calculations. In all four zeolites, 5-FU dimers are considerably more stable than individual 5-FU molecules due to attractive guest-guest interactions. However, an additional stabilisation of larger oligomers is prominent only for FAU, where the large supercages impose less constraints on molecular orientation compared to zeolites with channel-type pores. In the second part, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with classical force fields are used to investigate the diffusion of 5-FU in zeolites FAU and MOR. For single molecules, the computed self-diffusion coefficients are on the order of 1 to 2∙10−9 m2/s for FAU and 3 to 6∙10−9 m2/s for MOR. Dimers and larger oligomers diffuse more slowly. While 5-FU dimers and trimers remain mobile in MOR, trimers and especially tetramers in FAU become nearly immobile on the nanosecond timescale. These findings highlight that the diffusion of molecules that can form strong hydrogen bonds can be significantly impeded by attractive guest-guest interactions, even at very low loadings. Besides, the low mobility of larger 5-FU oligomers could indicate that kinetic effects are responsible for the large discrepancy between experimentally reported 5-FU uptakes in FAU-type zeolites and theoretical predictions.

item.title: The CPOSS Database of Computed Crystal Structures
item.description: Molecular crystal structure prediction (CSP) has radically evolved over the last two decades from a niche research topic to a tool for solid form prediction and derisking. The Control and Prediction of the Organic Solid State (CPOSS) project led by Professor Sarah (Sally) Price has developed CSP over more than two decades of research, generating a large number of deeply researched landscapes, populated by alternative crystal packings for a given chemical system, including structures and systems that have not been observed experimentally. Here we present the CPOSS Database of Computed Crystal Structures, a public collection of CSP landscapes developed within the CPOSS project. This public inventory contains 310 documented searches for 234 molecular systems, comprising 190 single-component and 44 multicomponent systems, with 517,594 archived structure files across 508 energy-model archives. Structures are accompanied by search and computational-method descriptions, tabulated properties, and connections to experimental structures and the original literature where available. The collection’s principal contribution is its depth of candidate packing arrangements for individual systems, together with the provenance needed to interpret successive searches and energy refinements. We describe the construction, coverage, access routes, and limitations of the public release, and discuss its use in physical chemistry, crystal structure prediction, and atomistic model development. The database is released together with an interactive CSP Landscape Navigator under CC0 1.0.

item.title: What Can the Records of Published Self-Driving Laboratories Predict About a New Platform? A Step-Level Database and Explorer
item.description: Published closed-loop self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are described in prose, so what their records could predict about a new platform has not been tested. I release sdl-workflows, a database of 237 SDL papers coded by a language model as ordered steps, each with an operation and the type of module performing it, and as connections between modules, each with a transfer mode such as fixed tubing, a robot arm or a person (2610 steps and 1681 connections). On 30 held-out papers, the records agreed with an independent coding by a second model (micro-F1 0.891 to 0.905). The release includes the timing data the papers state and an explorer for comparing platforms. A model fitted to papers up to 2023 assigns each connection the most frequent mode among earlier connections between the same operations in the same field. It predicted the recorded transfer mode of 424 connections in papers from 2024 better than the most frequent mode per pair of operation families (accuracy 0.512 against 0.441; 95% confidence interval of the difference 0.016 to 0.125). A model of the same kind did not predict the module type of 1189 steps better than the most frequent module type per operation. A discrete-event simulation predicted reported throughput no better than the median throughput reported by other papers in the same field. Its inputs are rarely stated: 23 of the 237 papers give the duration of every step. The prediction of module types and transfer modes is released as a benchmark.

item.title: Interaction without an interaction module
item.description: The prevailing way to model a many-body system is to encode every component and then let a module capture interaction. We show that the explicit interaction module is harmful when the number of components increases. We use a simple interaction-carrying encoder that compresses a component’s interaction contribution into its representation, and combine the representations by linear aggregation. This modelling approach is simple in form yet delivers unexpectedly excellent performance: it matches the prevailing explicit route under most conditions and exceeds it when a mixture carries more components than the training set covered. Moreover, an encoder produced this way has a clear advantage over per-component descriptors when it is transferred to a similar task: it greatly reduces the data requirements.

item.title: From Execution to Discovery : Physical Verification as the Key Gap in AI Agents for Science
item.description: Why can AI agents operate reliably in digital environments such as software development yet still struggle to achieve autonomous scientific discovery? We argue that this gap reflects not only limitations in model capability but also differences in how agent capabilities are externalized and how reliably environments can verify the consequences of agent actions. In this survey, we trace the technical evolution of AI agents and propose a three-stage framework of capability externalization: reasoning externalization makes knowledge, memory, and intermediate inferences inspectable; execution externalization makes tool use and long-horizon workflows governable; and world-interaction externalization integrates environmental evidence into hypothesis revision and action selection. Materials discovery provides a demanding testbed for all three stages, spanning literature-grounded hypothesis generation, computational design, automated experimentation, and iterative knowledge updating. Although agents can increasingly complete predefined research workflows, workflow automation alone does not constitute scientific discovery. Sustained autonomy requires agents to assess whether new observations support or challenge a hypothesis and to select subsequent experiments accordingly. We therefore identify environmental verifiability as a central systems constraint on agent autonomy: the extent to which an environment can translate actions into timely, attributable, reproducible, and affordable evidence. This perspective positions physical verification capacity as a key scaling dimension for autonomous scientific discovery.

item.title: Photocatalytic Reductive Elimination From A Main Group Centre
item.description: The development of “transition metal-like” reactivity using earth-abundant p-block elements is one of the most prominent and challenging goals of contemporary main group chemistry. This difficulty is exemplified by the key, catalytically relevant bond-forming step of reductive elimination which, while often facile for transition metals, is very difficult to achieve for most main group elements. Efforts to bridge this gap have typically focused on delicate tailoring of electronic structure, supporting ligands, and coordination geometry, a task that is conceptually difficult and synthetically demanding. Herein, we demonstrate an alternative approach. We show that photocatalytic reductive elimination from an already well-known P(V) complex can be achieved rapidly and under mild conditions, via a transient oxidation strategy analogous to “oxidatively induced reductive elimination”. This concept has previously been applied only to transition metal complexes but is now extended to the field of main group chemistry. These results demonstrate a simple, easily accessible, but potentially very powerful new strategy for ‘turbocharging’ transition metal-like reactivity at a main group centre. Thus, it provides a valuable new tool for the ongoing pursuit of transition metal-like catalysis using main group elements.

item.title: HTE-Guided Development of an Asymmetric Copper-Catalyzed Retro-Allylation for Stereoselective Methallylation †
item.description: A copper-catalyzed retro-allylation of homoallylic alcohols has been developed as a strategy for the stereoselective methallylation of carbonyl compounds. High-throughput experimentation (HTE) was employed to rapidly screen chiral phosphine ligands and Cu–NHC complexes across seven representative aldehydes and ketones, enabling the identification of effective catalytic systems. Subsequent batch experiments provided the corresponding chiral homoallylic products in high isolated yields (up to 90%) and with enantioselectivities of up to 83% ee. The reactivity was further explored with an oxime ether and an α,β-unsaturated diester, providing preliminary evidence for the extension of the retro-allylation strategy beyond carbonyl compounds.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Model Implementation for UC Irvine Dataset 322
item.description: The dataset, sourced from the UCI repository, underscores the value of open-source resources in advancing sensor research. In this study, raw sensor data were compressed using polynomial fitting (polyfit), achieving nearly a 100-fold reduction, and subsequently analyzed with the Isolation Forest algorithm to detect anomalies. Python libraries, including scikit-learn, were deployed in an isolated environment to ensure reproducibility and scalability. The workflow was further integrated into Microsoft Copilot, enabling natural language interaction with the AI agent for streamlined big data modeling.

item.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Disentangles Pore Confinement Across Multiple Zr-MOF CO2 Capture Targets
item.description: Pore confinement in zirconium-based metal–organic frameworks (Zr-MOFs) is often described using the cage–window ratio (ΓCW), the largest cavity diameter divided by the pore-limiting diameter (Df), yet whether this composite coordinate carries information beyond Df alone remains unclear. We modeled CO2 uptake, heat of adsorption (HoA), and CO2/N2 selectivity for 239 Zr-containing MOFs at two pressures relevant to vacuum-swing adsorption using structure-grouped machine learning with SHAP interpretation, reaching test R2 values of 0.77–0.88. Although ΓCW correlated positively with all three targets, controlling for Df weakened these associations and reversed their sign, while the reciprocal analysis left the Df associations largely unchanged and a difference-based formulation produced no significant association. Df played different roles across the three targets, indicating that the apparent confinement effect mainly reflects the limiting aperture rather than relative cage–window architecture.

item.title: Revealing Phase-Controlled Surface Structure in PtNi Nanocatalysts via In-situ Gas Cell Transmission Electron Microscopy
item.description: The rational design of catalysts capable of efficiently utilizing CO2 is critical for sustainable chemical processes. The Super-dry reforming of methane (Super-DRM), which couples dry reforming of methane (DRM) with the reverse water gas shift (RWGS) reactions, offers a promising route to maximize CO2 conversion. Modulating the crystal phase of nanocatalysts offers a powerful strategy to enhance catalytic performance, yet the relationship between bulk phase and catalytic behavior remains poorly understood. A significant obstacle in resolving this issue is obtaining atomic-level insights on the surface structure of phase-controlled catalyst under reaction conditions. In this study, we employ in-situ gas cell transmission electron microscopy to investigate the surface structure of faceted PtNi nanoparticles during Super-DRM at moderate temperatures (550 ℃). Atomic-resolution in-situ observations reveal that the reaction environment induces a pronounced nickel segregation and subsequent coke formation on the surface of disordered A1-PtNi nanoparticles. In contrast, the ordered L10 phase exhibits remarkable resistance to such segregation on its {111} facets. This structural rigidity effectively suppresses coke formation and lowers the kinetic barrier for CH4 activation by 27 kJ/mol compared to the disordered phase. Complemented by in-situ spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT) calculations, our findings demonstrate that the bulk crystal ordering acts as an anchor for surface structures, governing the catalytic behaviors. This study unveils a direct atomic-level link between crystal ordering, surface reconstruction, and catalytic performance, offering valuable design principles for robust intermetallic catalysts in CO2 utilization.

item.title: High-resolution relaxometry suggests the presence of pervasive nano-second sugar motions in a DNA duplex.
item.description: Nucleic acids are central to many biomolecular processes central to cellular life, yet characterising their molecular motions and fluctuations with atomic resolution remains challenging. We introduce high-resolution relaxometry, combined with high-field nuclear spin relaxation, as a powerful tool to probe motions in nucleic acids. After recording an extensive spin-relaxation dataset from 2 to 23 T, we propose a framework, within the model-free approach, that allowed us to identify motions occurring both on the picosecond and low nanosecond time scales. By integrating these results with molecular dynamics simulations and ensembles, obtained from residual dipolar coupling (RDC) measurements, we propose a time-resolved model that includes fast helical motions and slower pervasive sugar puckering motions. The approach outlined in this study also provides a framework for interrogating molecular dynamics in nucleic acids with spin relaxation experiments and benchmarking molecular dynamics simulations that aim to characterise dynamic processes.

item.title: Bridging the Literature-to-Laboratory Gap with Language Models and Active Learning for Reaction Feasibility Prediction and Autonomous Exploration
item.description: Predicting reaction feasibility is essential to organic synthesis, yet models trained on literature records often fail to generalize to laboratory data. Here, we present a two-stage distillation and adaptation framework that transfers reactivity knowledge from large, noisy literature datasets to small, controlled high-throughput experimentation (HTE) datasets, and further leverages this transferable knowledge to enable uncertainty-guided active learning. Literature reactions are curated and augmented with chemical reasoning to post-train reaction-specific language models through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), producing a compact generalist model. In zero-shot evaluation across Suzuki–Miyaura coupling, Buchwald–Hartwig amination and acid–amine condensation, the generalist model outperforms the strongest baseline by 41.5% in mean accuracy and 29.2% in macro-F1, while surpassing human expert accuracy by 8.9% and macro-F1 by 11.5%. To accelerate active exploration, generalist predictions are transferred into warm priors for Bayesian neural networks. This warm prior reduces the experimental labels needed to reach a held-out macro-F1 ≥ 0.70 by 25.0–42.9% relative to a vanilla Bayesian neural network (BNN). Furthermore, uncertainty-guided acquisition prioritizes informative reactions, enabling the models to approach full-pool training performance using only about oneeighth of the total available reactions. To our knowledge, this work establishes the first experimentally validated literature-to-laboratory paradigm connecting 1 large-scale post-trained language models with active experimental design, providing a practical foundation for data-efficient, privacy-preserving, and autonomous chemical discovery.

item.title: Inhibiting LINE-1 retrotransposons therapeutically in disease
item.description: The LINE-1 retrotransposon is a virus-like genomic element that can activate in diseased cells. It has been implicated in cancer, autoimmunity, developmental disorders, infectious disease and neurodegeneration. LINE-1 can be inhibited by reverse transcriptase inhibitors, small molecules originally developed for HIV. The correlation between HIV and LINE-1 inhibition is ∼0.9 on a log scale, in spite of >450 Mya of evolutionary history since retroviruses diverged from retrotransposons. Suppression of HIV requires prevention of a completed 9.7 kb virus insertion into the genome in immune cells. However, every cell in the body already contains >100 copies of LINE-1 that can potentially activate. Even incomplete LINE-1 mediated insertions can cause damaging mutations and genome instability. Furthermore, partial HIV and LINE-1 products in the cytoplasm of cells can contribute to an inflammatory immune response. Preclinical studies have shown LINE-1 inhibitors slow the progression of otherwise unrelated diseases. LINE-1’s contribution to these diseases can potentially be quantified using single-nucleus whole-genome sequencing on diseased tissue, enabling prioritization of disease selection for therapeutic development. Furthermore, LINE-1’s ORF1p protein can be measured in the blood of individuals with certain cancers. LINE-1 inhibitors could therefore be extended to various diseases. Potentially used both as an anti-inflammatory and prophylactically to help preserve genome integrity. Reverse transcriptase inhibitors are available at low cost for HIV, and higher doses of some could be used to inhibit LINE-1. However, reverse transcriptase inhibitors do not prevent DNA cutting by LINE-1’s endonuclease. Novel inhibitors may therefore be required. This, combined with novel diagnostics opens up possibilities for inhibiting LINE-1 therapeutically in disease

item.title: Cholesterol Condensation and Phospholipid Convergence in cis-ssPalmO-phe Bilayers: A Molecular Dynamics Study
item.description: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) deliver nucleic acids, yet how the ionizable lipid, phospholipid, and cholesterol organise the membrane at the molecular level remains unclear. Here, we performed atomistic molecular dynamics simulations of flat bilayers of the ionizable lipid cis-ssPalmO-phe (50 mol%) with one of four phospholipids (DSPC, DSPE, DOPC, DOPE) and cholesterol at 40 mol% phospholipid and 40 mol% cholesterol, with the binding free energy of cholesterol calculated using umbrella sampling. In the cholesterol-rich systems, all four bilayers were thicker (from 4.37–5.12 to 5.14–5.80 nm) and more tightly packed (from 2.02–2.27 to 2.60–2.86 lipids nm−2) as compared to the phospholipid-rich system. Also, in cholesterol-rich systems, lateral diffusion was 30 to 40% lower; cholesterol stood more upright. Cholesterol tilt and acyl-chain order became more alike across the four phospholipids, and the spread in the binding free energy of cholesterol narrowed (about 9 to 5 kcal mol−1) while its mean rose only modestly (about 13 to 16 kcal mol−1). Because the ionizable lipid (IL) fraction was fixed, more cholesterol means less phospholipid, so these effects reflect composition and cannot be assigned to cholesterol alone. item.title: Patient-Level Reassessment of Breast Raman Spectroscopy: Data Leakage and Limits of Subtype Classification
item.description: Reliable interpretation of Raman spectra from breast tissue requires evaluation on patients absent from model training. We reanalysed a public ex vivo dataset comprising 641 spectra, 80 tissue samples and 71 donors to assess the effect of validation design on breast cancer classification. In a GNU Octave reproduction of the deposited analysis, an indexing statement caused an average of 56% of testfold spectra also to be selected for training. With the original and corrected indexing operations, four-class support-vector-machine accuracy was 87.6% and 59.1%, respectively; the reproduction used an approximate kernel-scale setting rather than the original MATLAB heuristic. Under donor-disjoint nested validation, five classifiers achieved 55–60% four-class accuracy, with invasive lobular carcinoma sensitivity of only 6–15%. Cancer-versus-normal classification remained more robust (support vector machine accuracy 90.0%; donor-bootstrap 95% confidence interval 83.8–95.3%). A fixed-pipeline analysis gave four-class accuracies of 81.7%, 77.9%, 60.9% and 62.1% when folds were formed at the spectrum, measurement-point, sample and donor levels, respectively. A bandresolved variance decomposition indicated that donor identity accounted for the largest share of within-class variance at the carotenoid bands (1157 and 1525 cm-1; 58–63%), whereas class information was concentrated at the phenylalanine band (1004 cm-1). Donor-level band ratios differed between cancer and normal tissue but not between DCIS and invasive lobular carcinoma. Adding the highwavenumber region, varying preprocessing, or increasing the number of lobular carcinoma training donors from about 2 to 8 did not raise lobular carcinoma sensitivity above 25%. In a simulation of the measurement chain with real fluorescence backgrounds and Poisson shot noise, donor-shared backgrounds and collection gains produced little optimism after preprocessing, whereas donor-specific tissue chemistry did. Donor-separated conformal calibration yielded 91.0% empirical marginal coverage for the four-class task at a nominal 90% target, but coverage was lower for invasive subtypes; class-conditional calibration equalised coverage across classes but returned large prediction sets. These findings identify substantial validation sensitivity in this dataset and underline the need for patient-level evaluation, reproducible code and classspecific uncertainty reporting.

item.title: Ultrasound-Controlled Activation of Tetrazine-TCO Click-to-release Chemistry Through Sonochemical Oxidation of Dihydrotetrazine
item.description: External control over click chemistry offers opportunities for the spatiotemporal regulation of bioorthogonal ligation and cleavage, but the limited tissue penetration of light constrains photoactivated approaches. Herein, we introduce a new mechanistic approach to ultrasound-controlled click chemistry based on the direct sonochemical oxidation of dihydrotetrazine (DHTz) precursors. The precursors require no additional cleavable masking group, and low-intensity therapeutic ultrasound activates their oxidation through sonochemically generated hydroxyl radicals without the need for added sensitizers. A pyridinyl-substituted precursor, DHTz2, exhibits limited background oxidation and efficient sonochemical activation, while the resulting tetrazine product shows good stability under ultrasound exposure. The ultrasound-activated tetrazine readily undergoes ligation reactions with TCOs, including a TCO-DOX conjugate in which a bioorthogonal click-to-release cascade releases free DOX and restores its cytotoxic activity against cancer cells. Importantly, ultrasound applied through a chicken breast tissue barrier remains effective in triggering bioorthogonal click-to-release and activating the prodrug. This work establishes a new mechanistic approach that couples the fundamental sonochemistry of acoustic cavitation with the selective activation of click chemistry and bioorthogonal cleavage, providing a new platform for the remote, non-optical control of bioorthogonal ligation and cargo release using tissue-penetrating biomedical ultrasound.
